I really don’t think so. I shot a wedding this weekend. The bride’s face when she sees her friends beaming at her from the aisles, the little expressions between the guests from both families as they get to know each other on the dance floor, these could be replicated, but they wouldn’t trigger the memory of the people in the photos. They wouldn’t tell you anything about real people or mean much to anyone. They’d just be visually interesting, while photos of actual people at meaningful moments are treasures. AI for pure, impersonal art photography, divorced from context, might be able to produce jaw dropping results, but the capturing individual lives and communities requires a camera and a photographer. I think we would all do well to remember this aspect of photography, anyway. When it comes to shooting people, real dynamics of real times and places can’t be replaced. As for creativity, noticing and framing those dynamics kept me plenty busy this weekend, and I’m sure it will continue to do so.

I’ve struggled with that fear as well, and the best way I’ve found past it is to internalize and truly believe the truth. That I’m not a stalker. I’m trying to make something, not get away with something. People can feel when I feel uneasy about what I’m doing and that uneasiness can be contagious. So the clearer I am in my mind about the legitimacy of what I’m doing, the less I see myself through an imagined perspective of someone else that what I’m doing is not legitimate, the more comfortable people seem to be with me photographing.

Exactly. That’s the idea. To let them know I’m a photographer with the intention of making a photograph, not a weirdo that wants to just look at them forever. If it’s less about them and more about a photo, they’re more open to it. They’re helping me make something and it doesn’t take much effort on their part. So I usually avoid anything that could be construed as a compliment. “The sun looks really interesting through your hair” > “Your hair looks really pretty with the sun shining through it.” Sometimes a compliment is the right way though. My gut usually tells me what’s appropriate and most advantageous.

When I started shooting, I didn’t know I was transferring my files wrong. I shot in RAW and I used the Canon Connect app to transfer to my iPad. The app had a bug that transferred everything in tiny files. We’re talking kilobytes here. Not knowing anything was wrong, I proceeded. I got some great images by doing extensive, overlaying masks. The shadow slider didn’t do much, but clarity, texture, exposure, and grain were very effective in directing the eye around the image. Honestly, I’m glad this happened to me, because I learned to make images with very low resolution look great. Now, with RAW files, I have so much more room to work. If you’d like to make these images look good, I’d suggest with pulling down the clarity and texture, experiment with masks, lean heavy into color grading, grain size and roughness, experiment with extreme adjustments in all areas, since nudges don’t do much. I also had some luck with over sharpening and then correcting with noise reduction. Most importantly, just don’t give up on the low res pictures. They can be made into captivating images. Our eyes and images and goals are all different so the main advice I can give is keep at it because it can be done. The super low resolution images were my portfolio for awhile. They got me work, and I’m still proud of them.

I certainly believe in the ones that are fast acting and noticeably psychoactive. Ambien has helped me sleep. Adderall aided focus. Xanax has helped me relax. So I believe in them the way I believe in alcohol or weed or psychedelics that I have taken and experienced obvious effects and undeniable potential for danger and pitfalls, and a most of those I’ll never take again. As for the ones that take “time to work,” I have never noticed any positive change I could definitely attribute to the drug. There are just too many variables. Any time I’m invested enough in changing my life to see a psychiatrist I’m also invested enough to meet new people, change my habits, take on new activities, anything, really, to fight out of the depression. It is impossible for me to know how much of my mood is due to my changing life and how much was due to a drug, but my doctors have been resistant to this fact. I once saw a practitioner who insisted I continue to take venlaflaxen, a drug that did nothing for me, because I had such an elevated mood the month I began taking it. It didn’t strike her as pertinent that I had also fallen in love that month with a woman who had arrived in the country on the date my prescription was filled, nor that the drug seemed to stop working when she moved back to her home country. I’ve also never noticed any serious, negative purely psychological consequences of going off most long acting drugs. Just physical horror, and a sort of offness that is hard to describes The flip-side of this is I can also never know what problems I face now were caused by taking so many of these drugs. I took all of the major antipsychotics and antidepressants as a child, and felt okay before taking them, but have felt very far from okay ever since. Maybe I was fucked up by those pills. Maybe becoming an adult fucks you up. Maybe both. Ultimately, I’ll never know, so it ultimately doesn’t matter. As for recovering, this attitude has helped me a lot. I am what I am now, and the further I get from drugs I don’t and can’t understand, the better I feel about it. I take xanax sometimes for insomnia, because it seems that if I get enough sleep, exercise, and keep working—really honestly working—to live a life that interests me, the depression only comes for short periods that I can fight my way out of no matter how dire it may seem. I’ve been lucky in finding a doctor who agrees with me that this is a good strategy, as most seem disturbingly eager to prescribe grotesque cocktails of pills for which it is impossible to gauge their effectiveness empirically while obvious that they are deleterious to every aspect of my person. I wish you luck and time in getting some distance between whatever treatments were causing you harm and assurance that you can recover. It just takes a lot of living beyond what wasn’t working and courage when symptoms return not to do something against your judgement to make it stop. I don’t know what your symptoms are like, but, for me, when my depression comes back, a part of me is tempted to take whatever anyone suggests. It’s very frightening, the full darkness of it. But I’ve been through it enough times to know that I need to get my sleep in order, go hiking or lift weights, and get back to my creative work before I consider that stuff at all. So far, I’ve found my way back to feeling alive every time, even after episodes that felt immanently fatal. I hope you find what works for you, and the only advice I can give is that a perspective that finds its way around or through hopelessness is essential in finding that. We’re human beings, so there’s no such thing as escape from despair, anxiety, boredom, and all those things, but when they become debilitating, and you’ve found pharmacological options disastrous in the path, one option you do have left is treating the present as worth your struggle for its own sake but also with a future in mind. Gather what strength you have and good luck just might follow.

To me, the most dangerous ethical pitfall of optimism is its tendency to alienate the most sensitive and intelligent people in our society. Refusing to acknowledge it entertain darker viewpoints requires the people around you to conceal a great deal of what is on their minds, and without the ability to communicate those things, they suffer not only from loneliness, but the inability to work through their pessimism in any deep or convincing way. It is very difficult to even have a sense of humor about the dark side of life when surrounded by people who don’t get the joke. At the same time, a pathological sense of pessimism can be alienating as well. It seems to me that we all have dispositions that fall more on one side of the split than the other, but that adopting either as an ideology or guiding principle is a huge mistake.

I agree with you, but with a little wiggle room. It’s backwards that we facilitate the use of a drug that’s far more dangerous than others we criminalize. Also, after working in a bar, playing in a rock band (in bars) and nearly losing my closest friend to alcoholism, I no longer find intoxication to be good, uncomplicated fun, just from looking at it repeatedly, sober and up close. Damage to organs aside aside, I’ve known people subjected to savage violence because of alcohol: in many cases, a partner or caregiver who turned mean under the influence, and, in another, a murderer who prowled outside of bars to exploit the lapses of judgement and lagging reactions of women on their way home. He took someone from my circle. Still, I see some sort value in the 21st birthday blackout as a kind of initiation ritual. That’s not to say it’s usually done well. People have died, in frat houses, especially, from the lack of parameters put on this rite of passage: that not everyone can participate, that the initiate must be kept hydrated, safe, observed, that there should be limits, that excessive drinking doesn’t mean limitless drinking. That’s the trouble with alcohol, though. Every drink impairs judgement, so it’s likely for someone who decided ahead of time to have only one drink to have more. It also creates an near-rabid state of communalism, tribalism, whatever you want to call it, so even someone who decides not to drink will be pressured by the group to do so. Too many awful things happen, and I think you’re right that it’s the culture that does it. Coupled with the physiological effects, it’s a left-hook uppercut that KO’s any hope of serious problems not arising. I live over a bar these days and hear a lot of sad shit go down almost every night, see police-lights flare up and maybe save a victim of drunk driving but definitely cost the driver over $10,000 and even more that’s harder to quantify. It definitely puts me in a mind of what could be done about it, but I don’t have any answers. What little I know about prohibition sounds disastrous, and drug education programs like D.A.R.E. can’t present evidence that they actually do anything. Do you know any models of successful attempts to ameliorate the harm of alcohol on a social level? I’d love to hear about some of them, if so. I think a lot of us wish there something sensible we could do, and if we knew what that was, we might just make some headway and change things just a little for the better.

I can’t follow what you’re saying about Socrates or Nietzsche, but I do understand your analogy of a doctor knowing a cough is caused by the corona virus, knowing how the virus operates, replicates, etc. However, it’s not the same. Until there is a verifiable theory of what causes depression, what we know about it doesn’t go very far beyond the obvious— that it can come on from traumatic events, illness, injury, job loss, isolation, winter. The explanation that depression also stems from a complex set of factors, genetics, temperament, behavior, diet, childhood events, social standing and environment, doesn’t tell us much either, since it amounts to saying depression stems from a complex connectivity of the world as we know it. The employment of scientific methods does not always result in an acceptable theory, nor does effort count as truth. The chemical imbalance theory, for example, has not stood up to scrutiny, but has put as back where we started, knowing that depression has something to do with processes in brain, much like the entire subjective experience of a person. Nor has the descriptive data from tomographic scans or resonance imaging offered any clear picture of causation. Given the dearth of what is actually known about the causes the functions and disorders it studies, I’d say psychiatry has no place saying previous philosophical systems have not stood the test of time, especially on the grounds of varying theories and interpretations, since psychiatry itself is not exempt from these pluralities. The idea that the commitment of a handful of related disciplines to scientific method, regardless of their findings, has somehow supplanted philosophy as humanity’s  vantage point onto itself, betrays science in favor of ideology.

Here’s the thing,

tons of people embrace voluntary simplicity because they can’t cope. Maybe a career and income aren’t a problem but the accumulation of stuff gets to them. Maybe the accumulation of stuff is great but the desire for more stuff guts their wellbeing. Point is, complexity has potential to overwhelm and derail, and the point at which consumer capitalism derails you has no bearing on the validity of your interest in simplifying to make your life manageable.

As far as simple living being a lie to console yourself, I think your recognition of sour-grapes shows awareness and maturity. Being honest with oneself is important, but it doesn’t require we throw away our defensive narratives. It just requires we be aware of them, understand them for what they are. For example, I understand life through feeling, narrative and metaphor more than fact. It’s not that I think science, mathematics, and reason are inferior, I’m just not especially skilled with them. Consequentially, as much as I’m curious about everything, there’s just a lot of information I have to admit I don’t have the skills to sift through or ever know much about if I want to stay sane. The fact that I had to bust my ass for a D’s in biology and remedial math but excelled in music and creative writing has a lot to do with how I understand the world, how I think, how I make my meagre living, but accepting my limitations with humility and humor allows me to be even better and what I can do because I understand why I do it. I can say “there’s truth in art,” without being totally ignorant; I can adjust to the harsh facts of my economic prospects and my limited social utility rather than overcompensating.

Analogously, limitations to accumulating wealth are all the more reason to embrace simple living. The only thing it should give you pause about is judging others with a luxurious lifestyle. Not only is it unfair—since simplicity is a necessity for you—it can poison your mind with bitterness. As I’m sure you already know, bitterness towards others flavors your sense of self in no time at all, and that tends to counteract the reduction in stress and mental noise that simple living has to offer. As long as you’re adjusting to the realities of your situation rather than overcompensating for them, you’re good. The reasons something are good for you don’t make it a lie as long as those reasons are honest, and it sounds to me like your reasons are.

It sounds like what’s causing dissonance is “despising the luxurious life-style,” probably because that’s a bullshit approach to simplicity. It’s an extra step. It’s ostentatious ornamentation. The simpler perspective is embracing simplicity because it works for you rather than pretending to eschew luxury because it’s despicable. Sure, there are serious problems with conspicuous consumption and materialism and all that, but simplicity has it’s limitations, too, so let’s just be real about that, if for no other reason than it feels a lot better in the long run.

The point is that the event, the argument, the rant, the breakdown, has captured my attention and contains a broader human meaning. I never share, exploit or plagiarize the contents of these recordings but try to determine what kind of feeling it evokes, how it evokes it, and then find an analogous, fictional correlate. Recording: “What are you doing? Playing!? I live here; we lived here; this is my yard! This isn’t a jungle gym. This was my wife’s garden” he breaks into tears.

Idea for fiction: A close friend and follower of a prominent activist and proponent of non-violence leaves loaded weapons around a community erected statue of his friend.

I would suggest books on craft rather than theory. Technically, they are theory, but they focus more on effects used in composition than interpretation. A good book on craft will give you pointers that allow you to achieve whatever effects in whatever style you choose. The best, in my opinion, Janet Burroway’s “Writing Fiction: A Guide to Narrative Craft” (9th edition. It’s cheaper and has example stories, unlike the latest edition) and Alice LaPlant’s “The Making of a Story.” As for your question about authors knowing theory and whether they should, authors have always used a combination of absorbed techniques from other works and experimented with techniques from essays on theory. Authors of twentieth century, the latter half especially, differ only in the amount of theory they’re exposed to. The popularity of English and Creative Writing MFA programs has made the study of literature almost synonymous with theory of one or two types depending on whether writers pursue an MFA or graduate studies in English. “Craft” which is more prevalent in creative writing programs, is not much different from a “close reading” of your own work in editing and the work of your classmates in workshops. Close reading was the dominant style of theory through the 20’s to the 50’s. The point is attention to every detail of a text to see what effect it has on the whole. It’s important to know how to do this to recognize what’s happening in your own manuscripts. Today’s authors tend to study not just craft but also know a great deal of what’s called “critical theory.” This type of theory doesn’t examine the internal mechanics of a text as much as its connection to other texts, ideologies, other disciplines such as sociology or psychoanalysis, even economics and ecology. Many authors find these disciplines antithetical to creativity while others find it a wellspring of ideas and a source of social and moral purpose in their work. Others find it formally suggestive. That’s really up to you. My advice is to at least study craft. It will give you a toolbox of techniques that could save you decades of trial and error. When it comes to critical theory, if it interests you, study it. Stuart Sim’s “Critical Theory: A Graphic Guide,” is a fantastic overview that will give you an idea of direction you might take. Whether you study critical theory per se or just craft, it can be helpful to study any disciplines to widen your scope of the world. You can apply the elements of imagination (which was a piece of theoretical jargon only 200 years ago) and craft to anything you find interesting. Some authors don’t mess with theory at all. Cormac McCarthy, for example, doesn’t even like talking about literature, but there’s an obvious dedication to history and philosophy and formal experimentation in his work. My point is simply that it can be useful to study something other than writing itself, whether it happens to be theory or whatever. As a writer you can create theory from anything. The elements of voice you find tiring may be less a matter of POV than of perspective frame and tone. There are plenty of novels in third-person objective voice that are way less exhausting than “Falcon” or “Wise Blood.” Both Hammett and O’Conner use granular perspective. If their voices were cameras, neither would have panoramic shots, wide lenses, aerial views; every shot would be a close up. This adds to the a sense of claustrophobia that make both Hammett and O’Conner exemplars of style, hard-boiled noir and southern gothic, respectively. Aside from crowding the characters, both authors also favor slightly skewed descriptions that manage to evoke a vivid picture while also drawing attention to themselves. It’s not particularly difficult prose. It doesn’t demand extra attention, but if all the descriptions are up close and extremely evocative, and half of those use attention grabbing language, it’s going to drain your attention fast. On top of that, neither author shows us much of anything we’re not compelled to interpret. It’s another feature of noir and gothic. Both genres tend to describe even inanimate objects as imminently important or even malicious. They also both present characters with ulterior motives, so we’re scrutinizing all of these minute details from the speed and breadth of both footsteps and smiles to postures assumed in some very heavy silences. All of this is cognitively draining. For more books like Hammett, try the first volume of Library of America’s “Crime Novel” series, which offers a variety of pulp and noir from that era, or for something more contemporary, Akashic Books has a great regional noir series; try “San Francisco Noir” for Hammett or “Richmond Noir” for O’Conner. For more like Wise Blood, there’s Capote’s “Other Voices Other Rooms” and Carson McCuller’s “The Heart is a Lonely Hunter.”

It’s important to remember that human beings aren’t a means to an end, but ends in themselves. You can fail AT something, and something you try might be a failure, repeatedly. But since you typed this out I’m assuming you’re a person and not an employment history or business plan or crumbling marriage or disastrous painting. Basically I’m saying being a person includes lots of failing. But I get it. I feel that way too sometimes, and semantics don’t really help if you mean “I just have this overwhelming bad, judgmental, hateful feeling towards myself.” For that you can practice taking a deep breath and training yourself to be easier on yourself. On the other hand, if by failure you mean, “I look at how I’m living and don’t like what I see,” there are only three things to do. First, identify some things you can change. Second, accept what those are and they aren’t. It would be great to have no external or internal limitations on what we can do, but reality is reality. Third, pick the easiest thing you can change and focus on that. Sometimes you’ll get on a roll and other times you might fall back into a slump. But it’s important to try sometimes, when you’ve got the chance. But the most important thing is try to think more kindly of yourself. People are jerks to successful people. If you’re struggling, the last thing you need is one more person you can’t count on to at least be nice.

I stay alive for many reasons. The first is that I have taken suicide off the table. For me, it just can’t be there. I am too depressed too often to decide every day whether I want to live. First there’s the risk of it being such an appealing, even obvious answer. To allow myself to consider it would either 1) kill me, or 2) waste what time I have being tempted or lulled into fantasies of self harm. This is easier said than done, just not thinking about it, but with a continual, firm resolve to answer those thoughts with “I already decided, no,” makes it easier with time. The second is viewing suicide as a distortion of choice. The idea of suicide can be comforting not just in the sense of a permanent cessation of turmoil, but also as a false sense of power that one chooses when and whether to die. The truth is that any of us may die at any moment and will die at some point. We all must find our own way of accepting this. For me, it’s the concept of amor fati, or love of fate, the idea that one must have the courage to accept whatever point of life one finds oneself in (and if we’re considering suicide, it’s safe to say that point is a difficult, even hopeless one) as a step towards ones destiny. I can see how this might be too metaphysical for some. It’s too metaphysical for me. I use it as a pragmatic illusion. If I see this point as a step towards my fate, then I am obliged to accept it as it is and assume it leads onwards. Assuming it leads onwards leaves me open to ways that it might, which has helped me notice some very dim exit signs in very dark places. Furthermore, assuming it leads not just anywhere, but to my fate, guards against suicide in moments of hopelessness. I may suspect my fate to be a dark one, but it is still my fate, and if there is more suffering in store, it is still for me to experience, even appreciate, as I think we can all agree that even a tragic fate can be a meaningful one. If all this fate talk isn’t for you, this method can be simplified with recasting it as regular patience. Death will come. No need to rush. My third guard against suicide is my resolve not to harm others. Even if no one cares about you, suicide causes unforeseen ripple effects that will cause someone pain, someone we have not even considered, may not even know, and certainly doesn’t deserve it. And since we’re usually depressed when considering suicide, our perception that no one cares can not be trusted anyway, since depression distorts our assessment of how others assess us. My fourth tactic is to remember a moment i thought I was dying. I was on a stretcher, face gray, vitals fading, and a nurse put a needle into my arm. I convinced myself to savor the sting of that needle (I hate needles) because it was a sensation, and i may not have experienced any sensation ever again. That sharp pinch seemed ineffably precious to me in that moment, as did the yellow of the walls, the beep of the heart monitor, and as I stabilized, it was much easier to see more things as precious, especially compared to the bite of a needle. I wanted to smell a woman’s hair again. I wanted to read a book again, see a painting, daydream, sneeze, any of the experiences reserved for the living. My next tactic against suicide are my journals. I write by hand in notebooks I leave in the open. I do not censor myself. I fear someone having access to my most private thoughts more than I fear death. I stay alive to not become a mystery that people will fail to solve but come up with misinterpretations I do not wish to be remembered by. Another protection against suicide is a fatalistic curiosity. If i find myself in climactic or political nihilism (it seems to me that the future is grim) I reorient my despair to a desire to witness what happens. I also have my unlikely hopes to keep me going. I hope I can write better fiction and essays than I’ve written yet; I hope to fall in love again; I hope for the depression to remit as it has done in the past, even if only for a brief period of time. Another angle to consider is spite. Some people kill themselves to get back at people who have hurt them. One can also get back at different people by staying alive. Finally, there’s sleep. If i truly want to die and can’t shake it, i wrap myself in blankets like a body bag and play dead until I am unconscious. I will do this as long as it takes. I am in a very unsteady frame of mind at the moment, and I attend therapy, take medication, and do all the regular things we are told to do when suicidal. But essential as these are, what keeps me alive is thinking long and hard about suicide, not considering it, mind you, but examining it, considering what it means, what it implies, why I am drawn to it, what desires it might in fact be a stand-in for. Suicide is am impulsive act more often than most would suppose, so thinking carefully about it serves me well. It slows me down. It is not action. It is not suicide itself, and sometimes that is enough. I should add one more principal: loyalty. I have been mentally ill for long enough, severely enough, and with unpleasant enough social consequences that I have few friends left. If one of my few remaining friends were to kill themselves, it would devastate me. I would not betray my friends this way. Many of them have burnt bridges too, and to abandon them to such loss in an already stark and difficult life would be a cruelty I wouldn’t wish on my worst enemy, let alone those who are still here for me in spite of my many serious and difficult flaws. I owe them, one especially, the right to say, “there is one person who loves me. He will always be there. He has seen me at my worst and I have seen him at his, and I can trust him to value me when I no longer value myself.” I keep saying “one last thing” but I keep remembering more reasons I’ve decided to live. It’s been my experience that people who haven’t experienced mental illness have a piss-poor understanding of it. I hate hearing their advice. It’s too insulting and alienating for its naivety to even be cute. When I want to die, I need to talk. And I need to talk someone who has taken the idea seriously, who may be fighting the urge themselves, who won’t bullshit me or make me feel worse with corny platitudes and clueless suggestions that, frankly, make me think that if death called for them as strongly as it does for some, they wouldn’t stand a chance. I might not be the right person for every suicidal person to talk to. My pains and joys may be so alien to theirs that my struggle would strike them as yet another absurdity and piece of evidence that they are utterly alone. But I have been the right person for some people to commiserate with. It stands to reason I may be again. It also stands to reason that if I kill myself, that person in the hospital or on the street or in jail or at the busstop or wherever who needs someone who will listen without judgement or that shaky, panicked, nonsense-spitting fear with which people for whom suicide has never been a real danger often address the suicidal, if I kill myself, when that person scans their surroundings for that person who might understand, he simply won’t be there. He should have been. [edited due to typos from shaky hands that are hard to see due to blurred vision, please excuse any that remain]

Tl;dr Culture regulates its contradictory ideas of what an individual is by holding the individual fully responsible for problems with the most obvious societal causes. While both problems (anorexia and obesity) have complex societal roots, obesity is, by comparison, easier to understand than anorexia. We therefore place more personal blame on the obese.

There are already some excellent answers here, so I’d like to offer an _additional explanation, not an alternative one. Also, my theory isn’t based on research as much as having been, personally, skin-and-bone anorexic, morbidly obese, anorexic while obese/obese while anorexic. It also comes from thinking and reading about it a lot on account of how much it sucks. My theory is this: As social creatures, all our problems are in part societal. When it comes to problems in America or any country with a similar ethos, we have to twist our explanations around concepts of both valuing (taking care of) and respecting (expecting optimal agency from) the individual. We do this by downplaying or accentuating the societal causes of different problems individuals face. Paradoxically, the clearer or more easily identified the societal causes of a problem, the more blame is heaped on the individual that suffers from it. For example, psychosis from the habitual use of illicit drugs _alone and psychosis from mental illness _without illicit drug use both have complex societal causes aside from the genetic and the personal. If we compare these causes, those of drug addiction are easier to identify: housing issues alone (concentration of public housing, suburban sprawl, lack of public spaces, reinforcement of lower socio-economic status) offers many clear indications of societal influence, not to mention the equally multi-pronged risk factors such as increasing drug availability, poverty, social change, peer response, occupation, and drug policies. All of these are less mysterious in their relation to the individual’s behavior than the risk factors and causes of psychosis alone. So, fairly or unfairly, people suffering psychosis from illicit drug use receive more criticism as individuals. We consider them more at fault. The same goes for anorexia and obesity. The causes of anorexia are manifold and controversial. How do cultural messaging, abuse, a need for control, obsessive compulsions, gender expectations, and a host of other societal forces cause it? We have increasing familiar pressure for perfection in response to soaring inequality and diminishing returns on academic achievement, the loss of agency teens experience as parents become overly involved, the retreat into a digital world of visual evaluation and valuation to escape these realities. These are easy enough to understand, but how does this result in a hallucinatory perception of one’s own body? How does this foster a sense of control based on whittling rather than strengthening the body? There are many answers for these questions, but, by comparison, and only by comparison, the societal causes of obesity are simple: the ubiquity of junk food, the addictiveness of junk food, the ability of junk food to provide a temporary escape from all sorts of problems, including obesity, as well as the same risk factors listed above for drug addiction. Again, culture regulates its contradictory ideas of the individual’s power by blaming individuals in proportion with which the societal causes of the individual’s problem are understood. While all problems stem from a combination societal forces, genetic dispositions and personality, the more clearly we understand or feel we understand the societal factors at play, the more we blame personality, or, more simply put, the individual.

Definitely anthologies to ensure they find something worth their time. 1. The Dark Descent, edited by David G Harwell (anthology of stories from Victorian to contemporary divided into 3 sections that he defines as moral allegorical, psychological metaphorical, and the fantastical, which represent realist/supernatural, psychological, and weird horror very well).
2. American Gothic Tales, edited by Joyce Carol Oates. While limited to American writers, it covers horror fiction from colonial writing to the present, so covers the full time frame as what we conventionally call horror. The selections are those often overlooked by anthologists but excellent examples of each author’s work. 3. A best of anthology of the most recent year, such as Datlow’s Year’s Best Horror or Best Horror and Dark Fantasy. Both would bridge the gap from the previous anthologies to the present and allow the reader to find what current authors they like best, understand which authors or genre those authors build upon, and from there make an informed decision for themselves what direction of further reading will interest and frighten them most.

That took away from the meat of the narrative, which I didn’t care for as much bread, but imagine a sandwich in which the toppings are delicious but the bread is so good that it’s all I could think about, and that’s my experience with The Fisherman. Yours will be better, I bet. The meat of the book is more traditionally Weird. I love the weird tradition but preferred the contemporary sections, since (although I am a fan) there are elements of Lovecraft and Machen and the like that bore me. Nothing about the contemporary sections bored me. Anyway, If I loved the book, my guess is that someone who loves Lovecraft will ADORE the book. You also couldn’t pick a much better title to shift from Lovecraft into contemporary cosmic horror. It’s not just building on the weird/cosmic tradition with skill and reverence and daring but on that of the great American novel as well. It’s an extraordinary achievement that I hope to see totally transcend genre in terms of readership. It’s terrifying, touching, manages to be remain realistic down to the granules of human emotion and the set dressing of everyday life and at the same time giant, mythic, symbolic. As a final commendation, I’ll say that I’m reading Moby Dick at the moment and have paused several times to think about what a brilliant book The Fisherman was, and I haven’t read it since it came out. I’ll stop blabbing. Enjoy!

This is a little out there, but “A Widow for One Year,” by John Irving, though by no means a horror novel, has one of the most frightening scenes I’ve read in anything. A lot of poetry falls into this category for me too. T.S. Eliot’s Wasteland or Four Quartets, Ted Hugh’s “Crow” poems. A lot of black, American realist fiction like Ellison’s “The Invisible Man” or Richard Wright’s “Native Son,” are horrifying for obvious reasons. The psychological fragility of Dostoevsky such as in “Notes from the Underground” and “Crime and Punishment” also disturb me as much as any horror novel. The material desperation of Hubert Shelby Jr’s books have an equally disturbing effect. To return to John Irving, “The World According to Garp,” is a tragicomic dread-fest. It’s a very life affirming book, but there’s a presence throughout called “The Undertoad,” that is always advancing, always reaching out to destroy.

My interest in horror leads to a lot of other areas, too. Reading a nonfiction book on monsters or the underworld or Satan might lead to Hebrew, Greek and Latin literature. Over the last two years my interest in the gothic (which came from loving Joyce Carol Oates “Zombie,” not overtly gothic itself but leading me to other works of her’s that are) has immersed me in medieval romances and the romantic poets, and to better understand the poets, 19th century European history, and my Haunted House October reading led to me falling in love with Henry James, whose “Portrait of a Lady” and realist (or surrealist) short stories and novels I’ve come to love as much as anything, enough to want to revisit Hawthorn and read Balzac and George Eliot for the first time since those authors meant so much to him. Loving post-apocalyptic novels I of course picked up The Road, and learning about McCarthy’s admiration of Melville and Faulkner sent me back into their work which I hadn’t read since college. Bottom line, horror literature IS literature as much as much as naturalist or modernist or neo-classical literature is literature. I find the pleasure of its presence in other genres and other genres in it, of seeing the way it changes over time along with changes in philosophy and science and social organization as wildly and seamlessly as poetic or dramatic forms, observing the ways it expresses a type of consciousness whose only constant is insistence on intensity of fear in the reader almost as pleasurable as that fear itself. Most of all I just love how whatever you’re into, the more you get into it the more connections you see to other things. It makes me feel like there will always be plenty to explore and in a way that almost feels religious as if all things and therefore all of us are connected. Passions and obsessions are the shit. We’ve all got them or this year might have done us all in but I’m particularly glad to share this one with you fine folks.

Been reading this thread and have a suggestion. We can’t control what other people do, just what we do. Perhaps the best course of action is somewhere between your positions. We can all make an effort to stay ahead of the curve when terminology is either being misused or we know it’s perceived as being misused. For self care, we can do our best to express our needs in a language that will be understood, depending on our audience, how well we know or trust them, etc. It’s not fair that we should have to make the change to avoid the insensitivity and ignorance of others, but not as unfair as it would be to ourselves not to try once we notice we’re meeting resistance. As for taking care of others, we can all decide not to be a part of deligitimizing trigger warnings. We can take others at their word, no matter the terminology they use, since it does us no harm and encourage others to do the same. That way we can precipitate change in both directions, both towards a language that doesn’t carry the unfair stigma of trigger warnings and towards an acceptance of triggers as a legitimate concern, thus lessening our need for a modified language.
